title: Which whole answer is more likely?
hook: A model scores a whole answer by multiplying its tokens' chances. Which comes out on top?

knows: a model picks the next token from probabilities (next-word-tally)
that a whole text's probability is the product along its path (greedy-word-trap)
doesNotKnow: that because every extra token multiplies by a number below 1, the most probable whole answer is biased toward short ones, so search for the single most likely text needs a length correction

misconception: The answer whose every token the model is more confident about is the more probable answer, so 'most likely' means 'best'.
objective: The learner can explain that a 10-token answer at 85% per token (19.7%) loses to a 2-token answer at 50% per token (25%) because each extra token multiplies the whole by a number below 1, and that scoring per token removes this bias toward short answers.

claims.text: 0.5 x 0.5 = 25% and 0.85^10 = 19.7%, so the 2-token answer S is more probable than the 10-token answer L.
claims.source: Arithmetic; whole() in Demo.tsx; node 2026-10-14: 0.25 and 0.19687. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node: 0.5^2 = 0.25 -> pc '25%'; 0.85^10 = 0.19687 -> '19.7%'. The reveal uses rec, which check() sets only when L = 10 is complete; the question-case milestone requires that, so the reveal always reads 25% against 19.7%.

claims.text: At 85% per token, L beats S's 25% only up to 8 tokens (0.85^8 = 27.2%, 0.85^9 = 23.2%).
claims.source: CROSS in Demo.tsx computes 8; node: 0.85^8 = 0.2725, 0.85^9 = 0.2316. Stage lengths 1-10: 85.0, 72.3, 61.4, 52.2, 44.4, 37.7, 32.1, 27.2, 23.2, 19.7%. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Own node over n = 1..10: 0.85^n > 0.25 for n <= 8 (0.85^8 = 27.2%), false from 9 (23.2%) and 10 (19.7%); CROSS = 8. The reveal's 'At n tokens L won with x%' uses the last completed n <= 8, every one of which beats 25%; 'past 8 it always loses' holds since 0.85^n decreases.

claims.text: A whole answer's probability is the product of its tokens' probabilities, so each extra token multiplies the whole by something below 1 and can only lower it; therefore the single most probable answer tends to be a short one.
claims.source: Chain rule of probability: P(w1..wn) = product of P(wi | w1..wi-1), each factor <= 1. The toy's per-token chances are fixed and invented (stage tag 'Invented token odds'). | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation: whole(p, k) = p^k and every token chance is in (0,1), so each extra factor lowers the product; the stage shows this as the bar shrinks with each +1 token. 'Tends to' is the right strength: a longer answer with higher per-token odds can still win (n <= 8 here).

claims.text: Scoring per token (the geometric mean of the token chances, a length-normalised score) puts L ahead: 85% against 50%, at every length.
claims.source: (p^n)^(1/n) = p: S 0.5, L 0.85 for any n. Shown on the stage as 'per token: 85% (whole: ...)'. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Derivation: the geometric mean of k equal chances p is p, so per token L = 85% and S = 50% for every slider length 1-10; the stage prints 'per token: 85%' and '50%' with L marked more probable.

claims.text: Real decoders add such a length correction (length penalty or normalisation), because exact or beam search for the most probable output favours short outputs.
claims.source: Wu et al. (2016), 'Google's neural machine translation system', arXiv 1609.08144, section 7 (length normalisation in beam search); Murray and Chiang (2018), 'Correcting length bias in neural machine translation', WMT 2018. About real systems; needs the fact-checker. The brief's optional Stahlberg and Byrne (2019) sentence is not in learner text. | FC pass 35 (fact-checker, 2026-10-14): VERIFIED. Opened source: Hugging Face transformers (main, fetched 2026-10-14), GenerationConfig.length_penalty: 'applied as an exponent to the sequence length, which in turn is used to divide the score of the sequence. Since the score is the log likelihood of the sequence (i.e. negative), length_penalty > 0.0 promotes longer sequences'; default 1.0 (line 626), and the beam update divides log-probs by length**length_penalty, i.e. the per-token mean log-prob (log of the geometric mean). So a widely used real decoder applies this correction, and its docs state the reason (unnormalised log-likelihood favours short sequences). That exact search for the most probable output favours short outputs follows from c3. The NMT papers in the source field were not opened and are not the basis.

recall.question: A search keeps the single most probable reply, scoring each reply by multiplying its token chances. Without any correction, which kind of reply does it tend to pick?
options: Short replies, even when their tokens are less certain
Long replies, because they carry more information
Replies whose every token is the most confident
recall.why: Every extra token multiplies the whole by a number below 1, so long replies lose probability. Real decoders add a length correction, such as scoring per token.
